abstract: Supermassive neutron stars ([Formula: see text]) provide stringent constraints on the equation of state of dense matter. We report the discovery of a wide binary system composed of a red giant star and an invisible companion with an orbital period [Formula: see text] and a comparatively low eccentricity [Formula: see text] (with 1σ uncertainty). By combining radial velocity measurements from the Large Sky Area Multi-Object Fiber Spectroscopic Telescope and the Apache Point Observatory Galactic Evolution Experiment (APOGEE) with astrometric data from Gaia DR2 and DR3 catalogs, we derive a Keplerian orbit with an inclination angle [Formula: see text]. The unseen companion has a mass in the range of [Formula: see text] (spanning the full spread of all estimates), with a best-fit value of [Formula: see text]. This potentially places the unseen companion within the mass gap between neutron stars and black holes. Spectral disentangling using high-resolution near-infrared APOGEE spectra shows no absorption features from an additional component, suggesting the presence of a compact object: either a supermassive neutron star or a low-mass black hole. The wide, low-eccentricity orbit is difficult to explain through standard binary evolution channels, pointing to the need for improved theoretical models to account for such systems.
hook: A red giant's unseen companion may be a supermassive neutron star or a mass-gap black hole
summary: Radial velocities from LAMOST and APOGEE plus Gaia astrometry give a wide, low-eccentricity orbit for a red giant circling an invisible companion. The companion's mass falls in the gap between neutron stars and black holes, and no light from a second star shows in the infrared spectra. The mass has a wide error range, so its identity as a compact object is likely rather than proven.
title: Discovery of a likely supermassive neutron star in a remarkably wide binary.
